h: Darwin's rocks and hippos in Cambridge
p: Here's a name you'll know: Charles Darwin. Adam Sedgwick, the professor the museum is named after, taught Darwin geology, and in 1831 took him on a field trip to North Wales just before Darwin set off on HMS Beagle. Many of the rock specimens Darwin collected on that famous voyage are now held at the Sedgwick, which makes it a fascinating stop for anyone interested in the story of evolution.

The roots of the collection go even further back. A naturalist called John Woodward left his fossils and minerals to the university in the 1720s, and they formed the founding collection of what became the museum. The present building on Downing Street opened in 1904 as a memorial to Sedgwick.

Now for a fun one to blow the kids' minds. Some of the fossils on display are from right around Cambridge, including remains of animals like hippos that lived in the area during warmer periods of the Ice Age. Picture hippos wallowing where people now punt along the Cam and you'll never look at the river quite the same way again.
An hour or so is usually plenty, though fossil-mad kids could happily stay longer. Look out for drawers and cases that reward a closer look.

To round off the day, the University Botanic Garden, a short walk south, is wonderful for a stroll among glasshouses and trees. Or head to the river and walk the meadows out to the village of Grantchester for tea. The Mathematical Bridge at Queens' College is also close by, one of the most photographed spots in the city.
